title: Spells of protection (Kern ch. 21)
hook: protective chants for those who keep the sutra

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great tongue: the Buddhas confirming the teaching for every world to hear, and a week of lines gathered up. Your line: confirmed. Did one kind word get its action? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

Some words are said less for what they mean than for what they do. A lullaby hummed over a crib. A name called across a dark yard. The words a grandmother says when someone sneezes. Chapter twenty-one of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, is full of words like that: strings of syllables offered to the Buddha by bodhisattvas, by heavenly kings, and by a band of fierce female spirits, all to guard the people who keep this teaching. A new week opens with them. Today's word: dharani.
screen: `WORDS SAID FOR WHAT THEY DO.` → `STRINGS OF SYLLABLES.` → `TO GUARD THE KEEPERS.`

segments.voice: First, the givers. One after another they rise in the assembly. The bodhisattva Medicine King, whose own story comes tomorrow. Another bodhisattva. Then two of the great heavenly kings who guard the quarters of the world. Each says, in effect: here is a spell, so that no harm comes to those who preach this teaching. And each recites it. Second, the spells themselves. They are not sentences. They are runs of sound, kept as sound rather than turned into meanings. The word for them, dharani, is explained in the tradition as something that holds: holding the teaching in memory, holding the speaker safe. The chant does its work by being kept and said, the way a lullaby works on a child who understands none of the words. Third, the fierce ones. Then come the rakshasis, female spirits known in Indian stories for doing harm, together with Hariti, a figure the tradition remembers as a devourer of children who was turned toward protecting them. Now they stand before the Buddha and promise to guard the keepers of the sutra, and they offer a spell of their own. The very beings people feared become the guards at the door. Fourth, the Buddha's answer. He approves each offering. What all these spells protect is not treasure or territory. It is people: whoever keeps the teaching, reads it, and passes it on. Protection, in this chapter, is the circle of care that gathers around someone doing that.
screen: `THE GIVERS RISE ONE BY ONE.` · `SOUNDS MORE THAN SENTENCES.` · `EVEN THE FIERCE ONES GUARD.` · `WHAT THE SPELLS PROTECT.` · then, large: `PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: chant one protective line. Sit and let the breath settle. If you already chant, you can use a protective line from your own tradition; Nichiren Buddhists, for example, chant the title of this sutra, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. If you don't chant, choose a line from this path you already carry, like I do not despise you, and say it softly on each out-breath. Let the sound do its work. Don't reach for meaning. Just keep the line, the way a dharani is kept. The bell holds the time.
Dharani. A chant of syllables kept and recited for protection and for holding the teaching, offered in the Lotus Sutra to guard its keepers. Today's word.
Your line: protected. Today, notice one person who quietly keeps you safe, at work or at home, and let them know you noticed. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Dharanis are recited in Mahayana and Vajrayana settings, often kept in their Sanskrit-derived sounds rather than translated; in Nichiren Buddhism people chant the sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo.

original.note: Sanskrit: a chant of syllables kept for protection and for holding the teaching in memory.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dharani is a magic word that forces things to happen.
what it means: in the Lotus, a protective chant offered to guard the people who keep the teaching.
what a scholar hears: the tradition links dharani to holding, holding the teaching in memory as well as holding the speaker safe; the chapter's spells are kept as sound, not meaning.

notes: Paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884), ch. 21; nothing quoted, and no spell syllables reproduced.

Check the givers: Bhaishajyaraja, a second bodhisattva (Pradhanashura in the Sanskrit), two of the four heavenly kings (Vaishravana and one other; the Sanskrit and Chinese differ, so the second is left unnamed), the rakshasis with Hariti. Their number is left out.
Dharani as 'something that holds' is framed as the tradition's explanation, not an etymology claim; Keeper to confirm wording.
Hariti's story (child-devourer turned protector) comes from other Buddhist texts, not this chapter; framed as 'the tradition remembers'.
Practice names Nichiren chanting of the title (daimoku); confirm phrasing.
Editor: removed the unsourced claim that translations usually leave the spells untranslated (teach and myth now describe the spells as runs of sound kept as sound).
